To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the process of ‘ending AIDS by 2030’ is complex and involves a process of developing distributed efficacy which is an emergent, dialectical interplay that includes shifts in social relations.

the efficacy associated new social practices relating HIV risk-reduction is distributed amongst networks that includes mother—son and participant—facilator networks and includes a shift in social practices within these networks.
the process of distributed-efficacy, as we have defined it, is a dialectical interplay of agency and structure, which is complex and indeterminant.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the emergence of new social practices that facilitate the ‘distributed-efficacies’ that are associated with the ‘competent community model’.
the emergence of new social practices that facilitate the ‘ending AIDS’ ambition.
the emergence of new social practices in a community context and the role ‘distributed-efficacies’ play in this process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
‘distributed-efficacies’ are a complex, dialectical interplay of ‘agency’ and the ‘structure’ of social relations.
‘distributed-efficacies’ are associated with shifts in social relations and the emergence of new social practices.
the process of ‘distributed-efficiency’ is complex and unpredictable and thus difficult to manage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ‘competent community model’ is a useful tool for the facilitation of the ‘distributed-efficay’ that is required to develop new social practices.
the process of distributed-efficacy is a complex, indeterminate process, difficult to manage, predict or plan for.
‘distributed-efficay’ is a process of social change that is complex, nonlinear, and indeterminate and requires a shift in social practices.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is not only the ‘what’ that needs to be considered when designing programmes to address the ‘complexity’ of HIV/AIDS but also the ‘who’ and the ‘where’ and the ‘how’.
the process of ‘ending AIDS by 2030’ is likely to involve the establishment of ‘new social practices’ that will require a ‘distributed-efficacious’ process of development and uptake.
‘distributed-efficacies’ are a complex, dialectical interplay of social relations, modes of agency, and shifts in social structures and these processes are not easily managed or predicted.
